newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW - NZ earnings data seen as neutral.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - NZ earnings data seen as neutral.

text.p: Following are economists' initial reactions to New Zealand's Quarterly Employment Survey for November 1996.

Total average hourly ordinary time earnings rose 0.7 percent in the quarter and 3.5 percent in the year. For the private sector they rose by 0.6 percent in the quarter and 3.8 percent in the year, while in the public sector earnings increased by 1.5 percent and 3.6 percent for the quarter and the year.
ANTHONY BYETT, ASB
"Just a touch higher than the market had expected but within the realms of probability. I would not expect a significant reaction (in the markets) today.
"I guess it ties the hands of the Reserve Bank a little bit more, in the sense that there is that wage pressure and ... there is no evidence it is getting less.
"What we are waiting for is signs that that inflation rate is coming down quickly, or coming down. We have waited a long time and I guess the signs are still not there.
"Wage pressure is still there, reasonably high price increases are coming through on a quarterly basis, we know the housing market is fairly active right at this minute.
"There is nothing really coming through to say: 'Yes the Reserve Bank can really start easing policy now'."

But Byett said there was nothing to provoke the bank to tighten on these figures. He said last week's Labour Cost Index and the known increases in public sector wages, such as teachers' salaries, meant the higher public sector increase for the quarter was not a surprise.
DAVID DRAGE, ANZ BANK
"The bottom line is it's largely in line with expectations.
"Obviously we concentrate on the private sector -- we were expecting 0.5 percent and it's not too much at odds to that.

"With it largely in line with expectations, generally showing that wages are off their peaks in mid '96, as we saw with the LCI (Labour Cost Index) last week, it's really confirming that perhaps things are getting a little better on the wage front."
Drage said the data were not sufficiently at odds to what ANZ had expected to alter its view that there was some room for monetary conditions to ease slightly in the first half of 1997.
"We still see the scope for possibly a little further easing over the first half of '97, but that remains highly subject to the news on the inflation front," he said.
DAVID PLANK, BANKERS TRUST NEW ZEALAND
Plank said the data was largely in line with expectations, although private sector wages were a little higher.

"It was probably a number that reinforces the market's view that conditions needed to be tighter than the Reserve Bank said in December. Over the last few weeks, conditions have been the equivalent of 50 basis points, in interest rate terms, tighter than the Reserve Bank said they needed to be in December.
"Today's data will not change the market's view that conditions should be tighter than the Reserve Bank had said."

Plank said it was difficult to say what the future implications for monetary policy would be but that rises of 3.5-4.0 percent in total average hourly earnings, on an ongoing basis, would be too high for inflation to be below 2.0 percent.

"So from that point of view, if the RB thought that this was going to continue, they would be concerned. On the other hand, employment fell in the December quarter and if that weakness continued, then you would expect some easing in the wage numbers," he said.
BEVAN GRAHAM, WESTPAC

"Pretty much in line with expectations in terms of that total number. Obviously the public sector one was always going to be a bit stronger as we saw the rest of the teacher salary increases coming through there.

"I guess the private sector was just a touch higher than we were looking for...Generally I think it still fits in with the 'peak' story, that wage pressures have peaked. But along with the strength of the housing market that we've seen in recent numbers, I think it's a 'hold the line' policy stance we'll see
from the Reserve Bank at the time of their March projections (on March 13)."
